message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. These are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code) and common‑law principles. For specific situations—especially those involving disputes, evictions, or lease negotiations—consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Category | What You’re Entitled To | Practical Tips | |----------|------------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may hold up to **one month’s rent** for residential units (two months for furnished units).
• Must be returned within **30 days** after lease ends, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written record of the deposit amount and any receipts.
• Request a written itemized list of deductions if you receive a partial refund. | | **Habitability & Repairs** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural integrity).
• Must repair or replace broken fixtures, appliances, and address pest infestations. | • Report problems in writing (email or certified mail) and keep copies.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” remedy (see below). | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem within **30 days** of notice, you may pay for the repair yourself and deduct the cost from your rent. | • Keep receipts and document the issue.
• Notify the landlord in writing before making the payment. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or upon renewal.
• No statutory limit on how much or how often, but must comply with any local ordinances (e.g., rent‑control zones). | • Review your lease for any “rent‑increase clause.”
• If you’re in a city with rent‑control, check local regulations. | | **Notice Requirements** | • **Eviction**: Landlord must give **30 days’ notice** for nonpayment of rent; **90 days’ notice** for other reasons (e.g., lease violation, landlord’s intent to move in).
• **Lease termination**: Must provide **30 days’ written notice** if you intend to move out. | • Keep copies of all notices.
• If you receive a notice, respond promptly and in writing. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot interfere with your peaceful use of the property. | • Report any harassment or unreasonable entry attempts. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must provide **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes (under federal Fair Housing Act). | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) if you suspect discrimination. | | **Lease Terms & Modifications** | • Lease agreements are binding contracts.
• Any modifications must be in writing and signed by both parties. | • Never sign a lease that contains illegal clauses (e.g., waiving your right to a habitable unit). | | **Legal Remedies** | • If a landlord violates your rights, you can file a claim in **small‑claims court** (up to $20,000) or pursue civil action.
• You may also seek an injunction to stop unlawful actions. | • Keep all documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence).
• Consider mediation or arbitration before litigation. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – Look for clauses that waive your rights (e.g., “no right to a habitable unit”). 2. **Verify the security deposit limit** – Ensure it does not exceed the statutory maximum. 3. **Ask about repair responsibilities** – Clarify who pays for what (e.g., HVAC, plumbing). 4. **Check for “no‑notice” clauses** – Some leases allow landlords to enter without notice; confirm this is legal. 5. **Confirm the lease term** – Understand renewal conditions and rent‑increase limits. --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unresolved repairs** after repeated requests. - **Unlawful eviction notice** or threat of eviction. - **Discriminatory practices** or harassment. - **Large or unexplained deductions** from your security deposit. - **Complex lease disputes** (e.g., subletting, lease violations). If you’re unsure about any aspect of your tenancy, consider contacting: - **Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division** (for consumer‑related disputes). - **Local tenant‑rights groups** (often nonprofit). - **A licensed attorney** specializing in landlord‑tenant law. Feel free to let me know if you’d like a sample lease template, a more detailed explanation of a particular right, or help drafting a notice to your landlord.
